forces: Solo piano, ondes Martenot and orchestra
performers: Yvonne Loriod, piano; Jeanne Loriod, ondes Martenot; Orchestre National de la R.T.F.; Maurice Le Roux, conductor
intro: Jardin du sommeil d’amour is the sixth of the ten movements of Messiaen’s Turangalîla-Symphonie. Yvonne Loriod plays the piano and her sister Jeanne the ondes Martenot, with Maurice Le Roux conducting the Orchestre National de la R.T.F. on a Vega set dated 1962.

cues.title: Sixth of ten movements
cues.text: Jardin du sommeil d’amour follows Joie du sang des étoiles, a long dance, and comes before Turangalîla 2. The Vega labels give its length as 10′05″.
cues.evidence: Movement list and timings printed on the Vega 28.001/28.002 sleeve and labels (1962): https://archive.org/details/lp_turangalila-symphonie_olivier-messiaen-yvonne-loriod-jeanne-l . Joie du sang des étoiles as “a long and frenzied dance of joy”: Messiaen’s programme note for the first performance (Boston, 2 December 1949), as reprinted in Barbara Heninger’s note for the Redwood Symphony: https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/turangalila-symphony/

cues.title: Love theme, ondes and strings
cues.text: Messiaen’s programme note calls the melody of this movement long and slow, for ondes Martenot and strings, decorated by vibraphone, glockenspiel and the piano’s birdsong. It is the third of his four cyclic themes, the love theme.
cues.evidence: Messiaen’s programme note for the first performance (Boston, 2 December 1949), as reprinted in Barbara Heninger’s note for the Redwood Symphony: https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/turangalila-symphony/ Movement VI: “Here appears the third cyclic theme: that of love.” The sleeve text of the Vega set names the third cyclic theme as the most important and calls it the love theme.

cues.title: Yvonne and Jeanne Loriod
cues.text: Messiaen’s note on the Vega sleeve says Yvonne Loriod played the solo piano part at every performance, whoever conducted. Her sister Jeanne plays the ondes Martenot on this record. Yvonne became Messiaen’s second wife in 1961.
cues.evidence: Vega sleeve and labels, 1962 (piano: Yvonne Loriod; ondes Martenot: Jeanne Loriod): https://archive.org/details/lp_turangalila-symphonie_olivier-messiaen-yvonne-loriod-jeanne-l . Jeanne as Yvonne’s younger sister: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Loriod . Marriage in 1961: Los Angeles Philharmonic note on Messiaen, https://www.laphil.com/works/trois-petites-liturgies-de-la-presence-divine

cues.title: Koussevitzky’s commission
cues.text: Serge Koussevitzky commissioned the symphony for the Boston Symphony Orchestra. Messiaen says on the Vega sleeve that he wrote and orchestrated it between 17 July 1946 and 29 November 1948.
cues.evidence: Messiaen’s note printed on the Vega sleeve (English text): https://archive.org/details/lp_turangalila-symphonie_olivier-messiaen-yvonne-loriod-jeanne-l

cues.title: First performance, Boston, 1949
cues.text: Leonard Bernstein conducted the first performance in Symphony Hall, Boston, on 2 December 1949. Loriod played the piano and Ginette Martenot the ondes Martenot. Koussevitzky, who had been scheduled to conduct, was ill.
cues.evidence: Date, hall, conductor and pianist: Messiaen’s note on the Vega sleeve, https://archive.org/details/lp_turangalila-symphonie_olivier-messiaen-yvonne-loriod-jeanne-l . Ginette Martenot and Koussevitzky’s illness: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turangal%C3%AEla-Symphonie

cues.title: Love theme in later movements
cues.text: Messiaen’s note on the eighth movement, Développement de l’amour, says it develops the three cyclic themes. In the Finale he names two themes, a fanfare for trumpets and horns and the love theme, and bases the coda on the love theme.
cues.evidence: Messiaen’s programme note for the first performance (Boston, 2 December 1949), as reprinted in Barbara Heninger’s note for the Redwood Symphony: https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/turangalila-symphony/ Movements VIII and X.

cues.title: The Vega set, 1962
cues.text: The Vega labels carry the date 1962. Jean Roy’s guide to contemporary French music, also of 1962, lists Maurice Le Roux’s Turangalîla with the Orchestre National de la R.T.F. as a two-disc Vega set.
cues.evidence: Labels of Vega 28.001/28.002, (P) 1962: https://archive.org/details/lp_turangalila-symphonie_olivier-messiaen-yvonne-loriod-jeanne-l . Jean Roy, Présences contemporaines: musique française (Paris: Nouvelles Éditions Debresse, 1962), index of discs: https://archive.org/details/presencescontemp0000royj

cues.title: Quiet close
cues.text: The last stretch of the movement is its quietest. The sleeve timing of 10′05″ includes it, and Turangalîla 2 follows on the same record side.
cues.evidence: Heard on the transfer of Vega 28.002, face 3: the final minute of the track is its softest. Order of movements and timings: Vega sleeve and labels, https://archive.org/details/lp_turangalila-symphonie_olivier-messiaen-yvonne-loriod-jeanne-l

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Yvonne Loriod (piano), Jeanne Loriod (ondes Martenot), Orchestre National de la R.T.F. (orchestra), Maurice Le Roux (conductor)
fields.note: Credited on every label of the Vega set as “Yvonne Loriod – Piano, Jeanne Loriod – Ondes Martenot, Orchestre National de la R.T.F., Direction: Maurice Le Roux”. No individual orchestral players are named. Wikipedia’s article on Jeanne Loriod calls her the younger sister of Yvonne Loriod.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original 1946–48 orchestration, movement VI of ten.
fields.note: Messiaen revised the orchestration in 1990, according to the Wikipedia article; a record dated 1962 predates that revision. The labels give no edition and do not say whether the performance is complete or cut.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The labels give no session date. The notice (P) 1962 is the year of the phonographic copyright and first issue, not a session date. The table of recordings in the Wikipedia article on the symphony says only “Recording supervised by Messiaen in 1961”; no primary source for that was found. The upload and ripping dates of the Internet Archive item (2022) concern the transfer only.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Neither the labels nor the sleeve text name a studio or hall.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Vega (France), two 30 cm 33⅓ rpm LPs in the series “Présence de la musique contemporaine”, (P) 1962
fields.note: The Internet Archive record gives publisher Vega, country FR and date 1962, with a Discogs release identifier. The labels carry (P) 1962.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Vega 28.001/28.002 on the pressing transferred; face 3 is 28.002 face 3 (movements 6 and 7)
fields.note: Jean Roy’s 1962 index of discs lists the Le Roux recording as “2 disques 30 cm 33 t, Véga, 339-40 (mono)” and a stereo pair of numbers (read as 20.033-34; the OCR prints “20.033-54”). Wikipedia’s table gives Vega C 30 ST 20033/4, C 35 X 940 and VAL 127. Whether 28.001/28.002 is a renumbering or a later pressing of the same issue is not established. Both sources date the recording’s issue to 1962 or earlier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: 28.002 face 3: N° 6 Jardin du sommeil d’amour 10′05″ and N° 7 Turangalîla II 4′00″; matrix and take numbers not read
fields.note: Timings are those printed on the label. The transferred track of 10 min 13 s includes a few seconds of side lead-in and run-out.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation (Cebu scanning centre); the ripping operator is not credited by name
fields.note: The item sits in the Internet Archive’s University of Illinois audio-archive and John Rockwell vinyl collections. Collection membership does not establish the original session.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: From the ripping_date field (20220505). The sleeve was scanned on 2 May 2022 and the item became public on the same day.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable, Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge, Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp and Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; side recorded to FLAC and segmented into a VBR MP3 per track.
fields.note: The item’s lineage field states the signal chain. The final segmentation of this track is 3.995–617.415 seconds of the face-3 capture, edited from an automatic start at 9.411 seconds. Equalisation, de-clicking and speed correction are not described. The cut ranges are digital edits, not score alignment.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Messiaen died in 1992, so the symphony is in copyright in the EU, under the life-plus-70 term, until the end of 2062.
fields.note: The death year is taken from the Wikipedia article’s dates for Messiaen; the term is our calculation. Rights in the composition are separate from rights in the recording. No United States status is claimed.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: first published in 1962 (before 1963); US status not established.
fields.note: The labels carry (P) 1962, and Jean Roy’s index of discs, published in Paris in 1962, lists the performance on Vega. An EU phonogram published in 1962 had run its 50-year term by the end of 2012, before the 2011 extension applied (1 November 2013). The US term for a 1962 recording is longer, and no US clearance is claimed. The Internet Archive item carries no licence.

composer.background:
Olivier Messiaen was born in Avignon at midnight on 10 December 1908, and his grandfather marked the birth by singing the old carol Il est né, le divin enfant. His mother, Cécile Sauvage, had written L’Âme en bourgeon while she was expecting him. He later said there had been “only one influence in my life, and it happened before I was born”. At seven and a half, in wartime Grenoble, he sat on a bench in the town park reading the vocal score of Gluck’s Orphée and realised he could hear it in his head. “So, I was a musician,” he recalled. He also staged Shakespeare for his brother Alain, using cardboard figures and coloured cellophane from sweet boxes, with sunlight to light the theatre. Their father, an English teacher and Shakespeare translator, was away at the front. Olivier taught himself the piano. At ten, in Nantes, his teacher Jean de Gibon gave him Debussy’s Pelléas et Mélisande, and he played and sang it until he knew it by heart. Writing about himself in 1970, he said that the mountains of the Dauphiné “are his true home”.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1919, studying composition with Paul Dukas, music history with Maurice Emmanuel, and organ with Marcel Dupré. In 1931, aged twenty-two, he became organist of La Trinité. He kept the job for the rest of his life. The church divided his Sundays between plainchant, older concert music and his own compositions. At vespers he improvised, because the short intervals in the service left no room for complete pieces.
